bullets: How repeated samples, a surprise threshold and two kinds of error turn data into decisions: sampling distributions, hypothesis testing and error types
slides.heading: JC H2 statistics: sampling distributions, hypothesis testing, error types
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we build statistics from the ground up - a distribution of sample means that steadies as n grows, a p-value compared against alpha, a trap about what a p-value really means - and by the end you will know the two ways a test can be wrong.

bullets: Describe the sampling distribution of the sample mean: sample means cluster around the true mean and their spread shrinks by root n, so n = 25 gives one fifth the spread of n = 1
Carry out a hypothesis test at the 5% level: compare the p-value with alpha = 0.05, and name Type I and Type II errors when they occur
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting the trap that a p-value of 0.03 means a 3% chance the null is true.

bullets: A test returns a p-value of 0.03, and most people read it as a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true
The p-value is a statement about the data, not about the hypothesis - so is the popular reading right, or is it a trap?
slides.heading: A p-value of 0.03 - does the null have only a 3% chance?
slides.notes: Ask the class to commit to a guess before any definitions: is 0.03 the probability the null is true, yes or no? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because the trap scene of the lesson settles this question completely.

bullets: The sampling distribution describes the sample mean over many repeats: centred on the true mean, with spread shrinking as n grows
A hypothesis test compares the p-value with the significance level alpha: reject the null when the p-value is smaller than alpha
Every test can err two ways: a Type I error rejects a true null, and a Type II error accepts a false null
slides.heading: One subject, four tools: repeated samples, thresholds, traps, errors
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: every tool in this topic is a way of asking how surprising the data would be if the null were true - the only question is whether we look at repeated means, a threshold, or the two error cells.

bullets: Take the mean of a sample and repeat many times: the sample means cluster around the true mean
As n grows the spread of those means shrinks by root n: the n = 25 curve is taller and narrower than the n = 2 curve
slides.heading: The sampling distribution of the mean shrinks as n grows
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate what is happening: watch the five sample-mean dots pull in towards the centre as n grows from 2 to 25 - more data per mean means a steadier mean, and the spread falls by root n.

bullets: State the null and the alternative, then ask how surprising the data would be if the null were true
The p-value measures that surprise: smaller than alpha = 0.05, and the null is rejected; the animation's statistic moves until p falls inside the rejection region
slides.heading: Hypothesis testing: the p-value decides against α
slides.notes: Work the verdict in two beats: first read the p-value as the tail area beyond the observed statistic under the null, then compare it with alpha - p = 0.31 leaves the null standing, but once the statistic slides out and p drops below 0.05, the verdict flips to reject.

bullets: A p-value of 0.03 does not mean the null has a 3% chance of being true
It means: repeat the test 100 times while the null is true, and about 3 of those repeats give data this extreme
slides.heading: The p-value trap: it is not P(H₀ is true)
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: the 3% counts repeats of the experiment under the null - it is a probability about the data given the null, never a probability about the hypothesis itself.

bullets: A Type I error rejects a true null - a false alarm, and its probability is capped by alpha
A Type II error accepts a false null - a missed signal, with probability beta, fought by power = 1 - beta and bigger samples
slides.heading: Type I and Type II errors: the two ways to be wrong
slides.notes: Walk the four cells of the table slowly: reality across the top, our decision down the side. The two diagonal cells are the correct calls; the off-diagonal cells are the two ways to be wrong, and alpha caps the first while power fights the second.

bullets: Step 1: a population has mean 60 and standard deviation 10, so with n = 25 the sample mean has standard deviation 10 / root 25 = 2
Step 2: a test of that mean returns p = 0.03, and 0.03 is smaller than alpha = 0.05, so the null is rejected at the 5% level
slides.heading: Worked example: the sampling distribution and a 5% test
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name each one as you write it; say: the root-n shrink comes first every time, because the p-value is computed from the sampling distribution of the mean, and the verdict is always p against alpha.

bullets: A population has standard deviation 12. Find the standard deviation of the sample mean for n = 9 and for n = 36, and state the factor by which the spread shrinks
Careful - a classmate reads a test result and says: A p-value of 0.03 means there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true. Explain to them what the p-value 0.03 really measures
slides.heading: Your turn: compute, then correct
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them on the root-n shrink first, then on the exact sentence they used to talk their classmate out of the claim: A p-value of 0.03 means there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true.

bullets: On your own: a test at the 5% level returns p = 0.31. State the verdict and the reason in one sentence
Watch out for the trap one last time: A p-value of 0.03 means there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true. Say what the p-value 0.03 actually measures
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for a clean p-against-alpha verdict in your first answer and one clear sentence about data given the null in your second. Anyone repeating the claim A p-value of 0.03 means there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true. needs the trap scene again.
